The following defines the probability ranges considered when such language is used: Serious and Organised Crime Serious and organised crime is defined in the 2018 Serious and Organised Crime Strategy as individuals planning, coordinating and committing serious offences, whether individually, in groups and/or as part of transnational networks. The main categories of serious offences covered by the term are: Child Sexual Abuse Modern Slavery and Human Trafficking Organised Immigration Crime Illegal Drugs Illegal Firearms Organised Acquisitive Crime Cyber Crime Fraud Money Laundering Bribery, Corruption and Sanctions Evasion seeing money syphoned off through illicit transactions and cyber crime. In 2019, the human cost of this threat was brought into stark focus by the deaths of 39 migrants in a lorry at Purfleet in Essex. This was just one case. Throughout the year we have seen the impact of serious and organised crime in the violence inflicted on our communities, the thousands of drug-related deaths and the misery caused by the exploitation of some of the most vulnerable in our society. We have also seen the very real impact of cyber crime on our institutions and economy. Serious and organised crime continues to kill more people than any other national security threat, and has a corrosive impact on the UK and its citizens. Each of us is affected by it in some way. As a result, each and every one of us has a role to play in fighting it. Lynne Owens CBE QPM MA National Crime Agency National Strategic Assessment 2020 April A London-based cyber criminal was jailed at Kingston Crown Court for six years and five months for blackmail, fraud, money laundering and computer misuse offences. The offender targeted hundreds of millions of computers with locking ransomware. Blackmailed victims would be directed to pay ransom demands using a prescribed virtual currency, which was then laundered through an international network of financial service providers. The offender received more than £270,000 through this campaign of online blackmail. May Two men were sentenced to a combined 29-and-a-half years in prison for possessing and conspiring to sell handguns made at an illegal gun factory in East Sussex. The factory was uncovered following an NCA investigation in conjunction with Sussex police in August 2018 – the first time a criminal gun factory of this nature has been found by UK law enforcement. Officers discovered three firearms and component parts indicating a further 121 firearms were in the process of being manufactured. An additional 11 firearms made at the unit have been recovered since, with one known to have been used in two attempted murders in London. June A British-based Romanian national was arrested in the Netherlands for trafficking migrants. Dutch law enforcement intercepted the individual and, inside the rear of his vehicle, concealed in an area close to the bulkhead, found a total of 17 Afghan migrants. The migrants consisted of five children between the ages of five and 14 years old, a pregnant female, six males and a further five females. July The NCA Civil Recovery and Tax team obtained a Serious Organised Crime Unexplained Wealth Order – the first to be based solely on an individual’s alleged involvement in serious and organised crime – at the High Court. A wealthy businessman’s £10 million property empire has been frozen, with his property purchases believed to be funded by a number of criminal associates involved in drug trafficking, armed robberies and the supply of firearms. August An NCA-led, international investigation resulted in the largest ever heroin seizure at the UK border, with 1.3 tonnes recovered from a container ship at Felixstowe. The heroin had a street value of £120 million. Cooperation with international partners then resulted in the arrest and conviction of the intended recipients of the drugs in the Netherlands. September Two individuals were sentenced to a total of nine years for money laundering offences, as part of a multi-agency, public–private project led by the NCA’s National Economic Crime Centre (NECC). A major retail bank identified a vulnerability, whereby individuals were able to anonymously deposit cash in someone else’s bank account National Strategic Assessment 6 National Strategic Assessment 6 7 National Strategic Assessment 7 National Strategic Assessment Tackling the Threat Timeline of Success 14. Serious and organised crime (SOC) continues to have more impact on UK citizens than any other national security threat. It affects all parts of the country, having a chronic and corrosive impact on daily lives, businesses, public services, and national infrastructure. 15. The latest estimate available of the social and economic cost of SOC to the UK was approximately £37 billion. However, this is assessed to be a significant underestimate of the true cost, as the calculation uses a baseline of 2015/16 and does not include threats such as money laundering, fraud against individuals or bribery and corruption. 16. This year, increased knowledge across the threats has enabled an assessment of the number of individuals involved in SOC in the UK. There are estimated to be at least 300,000 individuals in the UK with a sexual interest in children. In addition, there are an estimated 50,000 UK individuals involved in other SOC threats. 17. The scale of the threat from SOC is growing across several areas. Victim reported losses from fraud increased by 38%, to £2.2 billion, in the year ending March 2019, levels of firearms offending continue to increase year on year, cocaine consumption has increased by at least 290% since 2011, while heroin purity levels are at a 10-year high. Detections of migrants attempting to enter the UK illegally have increased, and criminals facilitating them continue to use high-risk smuggling methods, as shown by the deaths of 39 Vietnamese nationals concealed in a refrigerated lorry in October 2019. 18. The threat from SOC is also becoming more complex, as criminals exploit available technology to communicate and commit crimes. All current NCA investigations encounter some form of encryption, and criminals use online services, including social media, to establish National Strategic Assessment Overview of SOC in the UK 4,772 >350,000 individuals estimated to be involved in SOC in the UK. organised crime groups mapped in the UK. 23. Many OCGs continue to be involved in multiple crime types. Even those that specialise in one criminal area – such as drug trafficking – are highly likely to commit a much wider range of offences to support their core criminality, such as serious violence, intimidation and money laundering. It is likely that the overall threat from modern slavery has not changed in the past year. While the true scale of modern slavery in the UK is unknown, potential victims identified through the National Referral Mechanism increased by 45% between January and September 2019, to 7,273, compared to the same period in 2018. It is highly likely that this increase is driven by heightened awareness of modern slavery among law enforcement, other first responders and the public. There are more potential victims from the UK than anywhere else, with UK nationals comprising 27% of all referrals. Offenders engaged in modern slavery are most likely to operate in organised groups or networks. While the majority of identified offenders are male, the proportion of police investigations featuring female offenders has increased to 34%, mostly linked to sexual exploitation. Offenders are primarily driven by profit. In contrast to commodity-based offending, in which profit is only generated once, the exploitation of victims of modern slavery provides continuous profits for offenders, as there is ongoing demand for the victims' services, such as sex or labour. Within the UK, social issues such as homelessness, isolation and substance abuse often contribute to victim vulnerability. Outside the UK, a lack of economic or educational opportunity drives the movement of vulnerable people. It is almost certain that non-UK victims of modern slavery are at greatest risk of exploitation immediately following their arrival to the UK. Although meeting face-to-face remains key in the recruitment of victims, offenders also use modern slavery and human trafficking National Strategic Assessment 22 The exploitation of victims of modern slavery provides continuous profits for offenders potential victims were referred to the National Referral Mechanism in the first three quarters of 2019, an increase of 45% on the same period in 2018.9 of those referred to the National Referral Mechanism in the first three quarters of 2019 were exploited as children (under 18).10 of UK police investigations into modern slavery in the first three quarters of 2019 featured female suspects, up from 28% for the same period in 2018. A number of signs of modern slavery offending may be visible. Victims may show signs of physical or psychological abuse, look malnourished or unkempt, and have few or no personal effects. This includes regularly wearing the same items of clothing. Victims may appear to be under the control or influence of others, rarely being allowed to travel on their own. to fraudulently apply for a visa 84 The threat UK demand for all common drug types remains high, while drug-related deaths are increasing. In 2018 (latest official figures available), drug-related deaths increased by 19% across the UK, including increases of 16% in England and Wales (to 4,359), 27% in Scotland (1,187) and 39% in Northern Ireland (189). It is likely that, in Scotland and Northern Ireland, poly-drug use of opioids with sedatives, such as Benzodiazepines, contributed to this increase. 93. Drugs are linked to a substantial proportion of cases of serious violence. Of all homicide cases, around one third of victims and two thirds of suspects are either known drugs users or suppliers. According to the Home Office's Homicide Index, the proportion of drug-related homicides has increased over the past decade, from 36% in FY 2008/09 to 47% in FY 2018/19, when there were 313 such homicides. Within the UK, drug-related violence is most prominent at the retail level, which is dominated by urban street gangs. Violence continues to be associated with county lines, where gangs and drug networks use dedicated mobile phone lines – 'deal lines’ - to take orders from drug users across the UK, typically for heroin or crack cocaine. Victims of serious violence within county lines are often operating at the front end of drug supply. More than 3,000 unique deal line numbers were identified in 2019, of which 800-1,100 lines are estimated to be active during a given month. Most of the estimated 1,716 OCGs involved in supplying illicit drugs supply multiple types, with almost one fifth involved in the supply of cannabis, heroin and cocaine simultaneously. These drugs make up 72% of all drug criminality. The cocaine market across England, Scotland and Wales is now estimated to be worth between £9.4 billion and £11.8 billion annually, and over £25.7 million daily. Cocaine consumption in these parts of the country is estimated to be highly addictive. Exploitation through drug trafficking – including county lines – is widespread, with gangs from cities such as London, Birmingham and Liverpool operating across England, Wales and Scotland. A young person involved in county lines activity may exhibit some of the following signs: • Persistently going missing from school or home, or being found out-of-area. • Significant decline in school results or performance. • Unexplained acquisition of money, clothes or mobile phones extremists make reducing the criminal use of firearms a priority for UK law enforcement. 104 Whilst firearms are used in a range of criminality, there remains a strong connection to drugs supply, with firearms often a key enabler for drug-related activity. Victims of gun crime are generally known to the police, indicating that criminals use firearms in feuds with other criminals, for punishment, or to protect or further their criminal enterprises. 105 A sizeable proportion of shootings are from converted, modified and reactivated handguns, including blank firing guns modified to live fire. 106 Handguns (pistols and revolvers) are still the most frequently used criminal firearms in the UK. Handguns are legal to own in many EU countries but generally prohibited in the UK. As such, they are usually smuggled illegally into the country. The second most popular criminal firearm is the shotgun. 107 It is highly likely that there remains a fluid supply of firearms into the criminal UK marketplace, predominantly through illicit importation. Firearms are trafficked into the UK from central and eastern Europe, often consolidated in Belgium and the Netherlands, before transiting via France. The most common importation method continues to be via Roll-On Roll-Off ferry – in cars, vans and lorries. 108 Despite harmonised regulations, standards and controls around deactivation, conversion and modification still vary from country to country in the EU. To mitigate against European sources of supply, the UK has influenced EU-level activity to further standardise and tighten firearms legislation. Police forces across the UK have reported commercial burglary offences by OCGs using specialist tools to force entry or make holes in the walls or roofs of Cybercrime is a growing threat that can have significant financial and psychological impacts on individuals and businesses. According to estimates, one million cyber-dependent crimes were committed against households in the UK in the year ending September 2019. The majority of cybercrime cases involve data theft, including CVV data from online transactions, which is also known as credit card verification value. This can be exploited by criminals through various methods, such as phishing emails containing malicious content, to steal sensitive information and make unauthorized transactions. Ransomware attacks are another common method used by cybercriminals to extort funds from victims. These attacks involve encrypting data and demanding a ransom in exchange for the decryption key. In one instance, a company lost €60 million in revenue due to a ransomware attack. Business email compromise (BEC) is also on the rise, particularly among small businesses. Cybercriminals often target employees or common suppliers by impersonating them and requesting payment of an invoice, which they then use to steal funds from the victim's account. The National Strategic Assessment 46 identifies several key areas for improvement in protecting against cybercrime. These include creating strong passwords, saving passwords securely, turning on two-factor authentication, updating regularly, and backing up important information. It is also recommended that individuals consult the National Cyber Security Centre's website at www.ncsc.gov.uk or contact Action Fraud or the police if they suspect a cyber crime. In addition to these general tips, data remains the key commodity for cybercriminals, and exploiting it can result in significant financial gains. CVV data from online transactions is particularly valuable, as it can be used by criminals to make unauthorized transactions. The scale of CVV scraping has increased significantly in the past year, with 962 e-commerce sites being compromised within 24 hours in one instance. This highlights the growing threat posed by cybercriminals and the need for businesses and individuals to take proactive measures to protect themselves against cybercrime. The National Strategic Assessment 47 also notes that BEC is on the rise, particularly among small businesses. Criminals often target employees or common suppliers by impersonating them and requesting payment of an invoice, which they then use to steal funds from the victim's account. In order to mitigate these threats, it is essential for individuals and businesses to take a proactive approach to cyber security. This includes creating strong passwords, saving passwords securely, turning on two-factor authentication, updating regularly, and backing up important information. By following these tips, individuals can significantly reduce their risk of becoming a victim of cybercrime. Fraud remains significantly underreported according to the National Fraud Intelligence Bureau. Reported losses increased by 38% in FY 2018/19, to £2.2 billion, with cybercrime being a major enabler of fraud: data obtained via data breaches, phishing and malware is used directly to commit fraud or sold online to other fraudsters. It is estimated that the internet plays a role in at least 54% of all fraud. Card Not Present fraud continues to facilitate other crimes such as human trafficking, with victims aged over 60 being targeted by cold calls from call centres in India or pop-up adverts on social media. Victims are often manipulated into handing over money or personal information. Investment fraud resulted in the highest total losses from victim reported fraud, with £338 million reported losses in FY 2018/19. One potential driver of this is the low interest environment, which has enticed victims to consider high returns offered by fraudsters. Cryptocurrency investment fraud remains an emerging area of concern, as certain types of high-harm frauds such as romance and computer software service fraud target vulnerable individuals by virtue of age, technological knowledge or emotional state. Romance fraud continues to have a significant financial and emotional impact, with reported victim losses over £60 million in the year ending February 2020. Criminals are experts at impersonating people, organisations and the police, and spend hours researching victims for their scams. To avoid falling for a scam, it is essential to: Stop: Take a moment to stop and think before parting with your money or information. Challenge: Could it be fake? It is ok to reject, refuse or ignore requests. Only criminals will try to rush and panic you. Protect: Contact your bank immediately if you think you have fallen for a scam, or report it to Action Fraud. For advice on preventing fraud, visit www.scamsmart.gov.uk. If you have been a victim of fraud, report it to Action Fraud at actionfraud.gov.uk or 0300 123 2040. Alternatively, contact the police or the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111 or www.crimestoppers-uk.org. metadata.title: National Strategic Assessment of Serious and Organised Crime

additional_metadata.General information about Best Practices:
The National Crime Agency has published the National Strategic Assessment of Serious and Organised Crime 2020.
It provides a single authoritative picture of the threat to the UK from serious and organised crime.
It shows that we are confronted with a rapidly evolving threat that is becoming increasingly complex as criminals exploit the fast expansion of technology to engage in illicit activity.
Their priorities remain tackling the high harm, high impact offenders who: exploit the vulnerable through modern slavery, human trafficking, people smuggling and child sexual abuse; dominate communities through wholesale drugs supply networks and the illegal firearms trade, and undermine the UK’s economy and infrastructure through their criminality, seeing money syphoned off through illicit transactions and cyber-crime.
additional_metadata.Time coverage: Covers 2019 as the primary reporting year and includes trend data from 2015 onward. Practices and assessments are intended for 2020+ planning.
additional_metadata.Geographic coverage:
Primarily UK, with significant operational collaboration with the EU Member States, the US, and international law enforcement networks.
Many operations involve cross-border digital threats, making the practice relevant to the EU and associated countries.
additional_metadata.Primary objective: To deliver a coordinated, intelligence-led response to serious and organised crime, with a specific focus on cybercrime, fraud, economic disruption, and online harms, to protect the UK’s national security, economy, and citizens.
additional_metadata.Secondary objective:
Detect and disrupt organised cybercrime groups targeting UK infrastructure and citizens.
Coordinate law enforcement and private sector intelligence sharing on cyber-enabled threats (e.g. ransomware, malware-as-a-service).
Reduce vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure and financial systems through collaboration and incident prevention.
Build capability across law enforcement and partner agencies through training, tooling, and operational support.
Support international efforts to dismantle cybercrime networks with the EU, US, and global partners.
additional_metadata.Implementation strategy:
Strategic Threat Intelligence:
Annual assessment gathers intelligence from UK law enforcement, intelligence services, partner countries, and private sector sources.
Operational Coordination:
NCA-led initiatives like the National Cyber Crime Unit (NCCU) and Joint Cybercrime Action Taskforce (J-CAT) coordinate transnational investigations.
Public-Private Partnerships:
Ongoing cooperation with banks, telecom providers, and major platforms (e.g., to address phishing, fraud, and SIM swapping).
Proactive Disruption:
Technical takedowns (e.g., servers used by Dried malware) and high-profile international arrests through joint operations.
Cross-agency Training & Tools:
Supports digital forensics, intelligence analysis, and cyber operations training across regional police units and public sector organisations.
additional_metadata.Success factors:
Evidence-led targeting: Actions prioritised based on harm potential, with real-time intelligence integration.
Integrated national response: Close coordination between the NCA, police forces, and cyber-focused agencies (e.g. NCSC).
Operational partnerships: Effective cooperation with Europol, Eurojust, FBI, and private tech companies.
Media visibility and deterrence: Major arrests and disruptions have reputational and deterrent effects on cybercrime networks.
additional_metadata.Challenges:
Rapid threat evolution: Constant innovation in malware, phishing, and anonymisation technologies used by criminals.
Jurisdictional limits: Legal complexities in cross-border evidence collection and extradition.
Resource constraints: Regional cyber units may lack the same tools or training as national-level teams.
Private sector reliance: Dependence on voluntary data sharing agreements may hinder full operational awareness.
additional_metadata.Alignment with EU Policies:
Although UK-specific, this strategy aligns closely with EU priorities and tools:
NIS2 Directive: Emphasis on coordinated response to cyber incidents and protection of essential services mirrors the NCA’s operational role.
EU Cybersecurity Strategy (2020): Common goals around cyber resilience, threat disruption, and international partnerships.
EU Law Enforcement Training Scheme (CEPOL): Echoed in NCA’s cross-force training efforts and threat intelligence capabilities.
Cyber Diplomacy Toolbox: Comparable in its use of law enforcement tools to impose consequences on cybercriminal actors.
additional_metadata.Transferability:
Highly transferable model for EU and associated countries:
Modular threat assessment design can be adapted at national or regional levels.
Public-private cooperation frameworks are reusable in finance, healthcare, telecom, and e-commerce sectors.
Operational playbooks (e.g., ransomware takedowns, phishing infrastructure tracing) can support EU-level joint actions.
Relevant for CERTs, law enforcement, cybercrime units, and digital evidence policy-makers.
additional_metadata.Comment: This places the IBM X-Force Threat Intelligence Index practice at an exceptionally high level of strategic value, combining technical robustness, broad applicability, and strong ethical grounding. It is one of the most transferable and impactful practices evaluated under your framework.
